title: Trees in the city: Valuing street trees in Portland, Oregon
authors: Geoffrey H. Donovan, David T. Butry
impact: Street trees add $8,870 on average to a house sale price (about 3.0% of median price) and reduce time on market by 1.7 days; a tree with 312 sq ft of canopy adds $7,130 to the house it fronts and $12,828 to neighboring houses (full text).
citation: Geoffrey H. Donovan, David T. Butry (2010). Trees in the city: Valuing street trees in Portland, Oregon. Landscape and Urban Planning. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.landurbplan.2009.07.019
takeaway: Source quote: street trees add $8870 to sales price and reduce TOM by 1.7 days

verification.evidence_quote: street trees add $8870 to sales price and reduce TOM by 1.7 days

title: The value of urban tree cover: A hedonic property price model in Ramsey and Dakota Counties, Minnesota, USA
authors: Heather Sander, Stephen Polasky, Robert G. Haight
impact: A 10% increase in tree cover within 100 m raises average home sale price by $1,371 (0.48%); within 250 m by $836 (0.29%).

takeaway: Source quote: A 10% increase in tree cover within 100 m increases average home sale price by $1371 (0.48%) and within 250 m increases sale price by $836 (0.29%)

verification.evidence_quote: A 10% increase in tree cover within 100 m increases average home sale price by $1371 (0.48%) and within 250 m increases sale price by $836 (0.29%)

title: Children living in areas with more street trees have lower prevalence of asthma
authors: G S Lovasi, J W Quinn, K M Neckerman et al.
journal: Journal of Epidemiology and Community Health
geography: New York City (42 health service catchment areas)
impact: Street tree density 1 SD higher (343 trees/km2) was associated with lower early-childhood asthma prevalence (RR 0.71, 95% CI 0.64 to 0.79) but not with asthma hospitalisations; association, not proof of cause.
citation: G S Lovasi, J W Quinn, K M Neckerman et al. (2008). Children living in areas with more street trees have lower prevalence of asthma. Journal of Epidemiology and Community Health. https://doi.org/10.1136/jech.2007.071894
takeaway: Source quote: an increase in tree density of 1 standard deviation (SD, 343 trees/km2) was associated with a lower prevalence of asthma (RR, 0.71 per SD of tree density; 95% CI, 0.64 to 0.79)

verification.evidence_quote: an increase in tree density of 1 standard deviation (SD, 343 trees/km2) was associated with a lower prevalence of asthma (RR, 0.71 per SD of tree density; 95% CI, 0.64 to 0.79)

title: The High Line Park and Timing of Capitalization of Public Goods
journal: Working paper, UC San Diego Department of Economics, December 20, 2014
impact: Home values within one-third of a mile of the High Line increased 10% immediately after it opened (2009); the author notes the city had spent $115 million building the park as of 2011.
citation: Levere, M. (2014). The High Line Park and Timing of Capitalization of Public Goods. UC San Diego working paper, December 20, 2014.
takeaway: Source quote: Home values within one-third of a mile of the park increased 10% immediately following its opening.

verification.evidence_quote: Home values within one-third of a mile of the park increased 10% immediately following its opening.

title: Sustainable for whom? Green urban development, environmental gentrification, and the Atlanta Beltline
impact: From 2011 to 2015, depending on the Beltline segment, home values within a half mile rose 17.9 to 26.6 percent more than elsewhere.
citation: Dan Immergluck, Tharunya Balan (2018). Sustainable for whom? Green urban development, environmental gentrification, and the Atlanta Beltline. Urban Geography. https://doi.org/10.1080/02723638.2017.1360041
takeaway: Source quote: From 2011 to 2015, depending on the segment of the Beltline, values rose between 17.9 percent and 26.6 percent more for homes within a half-mile of the Beltline than elsewhere.

verification.evidence_quote: From 2011 to 2015, depending on the segment of the Beltline, values rose between 17.9 percent and 26.6 percent more for homes within a half-mile of the Beltline than elsewhere.

title: Measuring the Impact of The 606: Understanding How a Large Public Investment Impacted the Surrounding Community
authors: Institute for Housing Studies at DePaul University
journal: Institute for Housing Studies report, November 1, 2016
impact: In 606 West (lower-income side) buyers paid a 22.3 percent price premium for properties within one-fifth of a mile of The 606; in the already strong 606 East market the trail had a very limited effect.
citation: Institute for Housing Studies at DePaul University (2016). Measuring the Impact of The 606. November 1, 2016.

title: The Impact of Parks on Property Values: A Review of the Empirical Evidence
geography: Review of about 30 US and other studies
impact: Review of about 30 studies: a 20% increase in value for property abutting a passive park is a reasonable starting point; near heavily used active parks the increment may reach 10% two or three blocks away.
citation: John L. Crompton (2001). The Impact of Parks on Property Values: A Review of the Empirical Evidence. Journal of Leisure Research. https://doi.org/10.1080/00222216.2001.11949928
takeaway: Source quote: a positive impact of 20% on property values abutting or fronting a passive park area is a reasonable starting point

verification.evidence_quote: a positive impact of 20% on property values abutting or fronting a passive park area is a reasonable starting point

title: The Impact of Greenways on Property Values: Evidence from Austin, Texas

takeaway: Effect size not confirmed from the abstract; see the source.

verification.evidence_quote: Adjacency to a greenbelt produced significant property value premiums in two of three neighborhoods.

journal: Transportation Research Record: Journal of the Transportation Research Board
impact: Hedonic models for Santa Clara County, California: about 23% capitalization for a typical commercial parcel near a light rail stop, and more than 120% for commercial land in a business district within 0.25 mi of a commuter rail station.

takeaway: Source quote: substantial capitalization benefits were found, on the order of 23% for a typical commercial parcel near a light rail transit stop and more than 120% for commercial land in a business district and within 0.25 mi of a commuter rail station

title: The Walkability Premium in Commercial Real Estate Investments
impact: Across more than 4,200 office, apartment, retail and industrial properties (2001-2008), a 10-point rise in Walk Score raised values by 1-9% depending on property type; no effect on industrial properties.
citation: Gary Pivo, Jeffrey D. Fisher (2011). The Walkability Premium in Commercial Real Estate Investments. Real Estate Economics. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-6229.2010.00296.x

title: Citywide cluster randomized trial to restore blighted vacant land and its effects on violence, crime, and fear
authors: Charles C. Branas, Eugenia South, Michelle C. Kondo et al.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
impact: In neighborhoods below the poverty line, treating vacant lots was followed by reductions in crime overall (-13.3%), gun violence (-29.1%), burglary (-21.9%) and nuisances (-30.3%); nearby residents reported less fear (cluster randomized trial, 541 lots).
citation: Charles C. Branas, Eugenia South, Michelle C. Kondo et al. (2018). Citywide cluster randomized trial to restore blighted vacant land and its effects on violence, crime, and fear. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1718503115
takeaway: Source quote: Significant reductions in crime overall (-13.3%, P < 0.01), gun violence (-29.1%, P < 0.001), burglary (-21.9%, P < 0.001), and nuisances (-30.3%, P < 0.05) were also found after the treatment of vacant lots in neighborhoods below the poverty line.

verification.evidence_quote: Significant reductions in crime overall (-13.3%, P < 0.01), gun violence (-29.1%, P < 0.001), burglary (-21.9%, P < 0.001), and nuisances (-30.3%, P < 0.05) were also found after the treatment of vacant lots in neighborhoods below the poverty line.
